title: Questions and negation
intro: This unit turns statements into negatives and questions. *däl* says what something is not. The ending `-mY`, written onto the word, asks a yes-no question. Question words ask who, what, which, when and why, and they need no ending at all. You will also answer, and say **too** with *hem*.

blocks.text: To say that someone or something is **not** something, put *däl* after the word you negate: *Men talyp* (I am a student) becomes *Men talyp däl* (I am not a student). *däl* is a word of its own and never changes its shape. It is the same after every pronoun, and the pronoun stays, just as in the short form of **to be** in [A1 unit 3](a1-u03).

rows.en: he or she is not tired
you are not tired (plural or polite)

items.en: This isn't a book, it's a notebook.
The book isn't new, but it's beautiful.

blocks.text: Many describing words come in pairs, and *däl* lets you use either half: *gyzgyn* (hot) and *sowuk* (cold), *uzyn* (long) and *gysga* (short), *arzan* (cheap) and *gymmat* (expensive), *aňsat* (easy) and *kyn* (difficult), *gowy* (good) and *erbet* (bad). *Erbet däl*, not bad, is the reply you met in [A1 unit 1](a1-u01).

**däl or ýok?** Both turn up where English says **no** or **not**, but they do different jobs. *Ýok* answers a question (**no**), and from [A1 unit 5](a1-u05) on it says that something **isn't there**. *däl* negates a description: *Bu kitap däl*, this isn't a book.

**What you will also see.** In careful style, *däl* takes `-dYr` in the third person, like any description: *Ol talyp däldir*. And in the second person a personal ending can follow it: *Sen ýadaw dälsiň*, *Siz ýadaw dälsiňiz*. The short form with the pronoun is right everywhere, and it is the one this course uses.

blocks.title: No, not
blocks.text: To answer **no**, start with *Ýok*, then give the sentence with *däl*: *Ýok, men talyp däl.* *däl* on its own is not an answer.

To ask a yes-no question, add `-mY` to the word you are asking about. It is written **onto the word**, with no space: *Sen ýadaw* (you are tired) becomes *Sen ýadawmy?* (are you tired?). Nothing else in the sentence changes, and the word order stays the same. Your voice rises on the particle, as at the end of an English question.

Like the endings of [A1 unit 2](a1-u02), the particle follows the last vowel of the word: *-my* after a back vowel (*a, o, u, y*), *-mi* after a front one (*e, ä, i, ö, ü*). Its own vowel never becomes *u* or *ü*.

blocks.text: **After däl.** *däl* takes the particle too: *dälmi?* This asks a negative question: *Sen talyp dälmi?* Aren't you a student?

**Which word?** The particle goes on the word you are really asking about. Usually that is the description at the end: *Merdan mugallymmy?* asks what Merdan does. To ask **who** it is, put it on the name: *Merdanmy?* Is it Merdan? That is what you say when someone knocks, or on the phone. In the same way, *Senmi?* means **is that you?**

**gowy.** With *gowy* (good), the *y* of the second syllable rounds once something follows it, as you saw in [A1 unit 3](a1-u03): *gowumy?* In print you will also find *gowymy?*. This course accepts both.

blocks.title: You may also hear
blocks.text: In formal speech an ending for **you** can follow the particle: *Siz taýýarmysyňyz?*, *Sen taýýarmysyň?* You only need to recognize these. The short form *Siz taýýarmy?* is always right.

blocks.title: One word, not two
blocks.text: Never write the particle apart: *ýadawmy*, not `ýadaw my`. In this course, a particle typed as a separate word is marked **almost**, with a reminder.

To ask for information, use a question word. It goes where the answer will go, which is usually just before the end of the sentence: *Bu kim?* (Who is this?) is answered by *Bu Aýna.* (This is Aýna.) *Sapak haçan?* (When is the lesson?) is answered by *Sapak ertir.* (The lesson is tomorrow.)

Meaning
Example
rows: how; what … like; what kind of

items.en: Who is this? — This is Merdan.
What's the weather like? — It's cold.

blocks.text: *nähili* asks **how** (*Ýagdaýlaryň nähili?*, from [A1 unit 1](a1-u01)) and also **what kind of**: *Ol nähili adam?* What kind of person is he? *näçe* asks **how many** or **how much**: *Bu näçe manat?* The manat is the money of Turkmenistan.

To answer **why**, start with *sebäbi*, because: *Men ýadaw, sebäbi sapak kyn.* I'm tired because the lesson is hard. You met *nireli* (where from) in [A1 unit 3](a1-u03); *nirede* (where) comes in [A1 unit 5](a1-u05).

blocks.title: No -mY with a question word
blocks.text: A question word already makes the sentence a question, so it takes no `-mY`: *Bu kim?*, never `Bu kimmi?`; *Bu näme?*, never `Bu nämemi?`

Answer a yes-no question with *Hawa* (yes) or *Ýok* (no), and usually repeat the description. For **no**, the description takes *däl*: *Sen ýadawmy? — Hawa, ýadaw.* or *Ýok, ýadaw däl.* For a firm yes, say *Elbetde*: of course.

lines.en: Yes, I'm ready. Are you ready too?
No, I'm not ready. I'm busy.

blocks.text: *şeýle* means **so** or **like that**. *Hawa, şeýle* means **yes, that's right**, and *Şeýlemi?* means **really? is that so?** To say something is right or wrong, use *dogry* (right, correct) and *ýalňyş* (wrong): *Bu dogry.* *Bu dogry däl.*

items.en: Are you a student? — Yes, I'm a student.
Is the tea hot? — No, it isn't hot.
Are you a teacher? — Yes, that's right.

blocks.text: **The tag dälmi?** To check something you believe, say it and add *dälmi?*, like English **isn't it?** or **aren't you?**: *Sen talyp, dälmi?* You're a student, aren't you? The longer *şeýle dälmi?* means **isn't that so?**

blocks.title: Answering a negative question
blocks.text: With a negative question (*Sen ýadaw dälmi?*), a full answer leaves no doubt: *Ýok, ýadaw däl* (no, I'm not tired) or *Hawa, ýadaw* (yes, I am tired).

*hem* means **also** or **too**. It comes right after the word it adds to: *Men hem talyp*, I'm a student too. With the pronouns, *hem* usually shortens to *-em* and joins the word, written as one: *menem*, *senem*, *bizem*, *sizem*.

items.en: Merdan is a student, and Aýna is a student too.

blocks.text: **hem … hem.** Two of them, each in front of its word, mean **both … and**: *Ol hem mugallym, hem talyp.* She is both a teacher and a student. *Kitap hem täze, hem arzan.* The book is both new and cheap.
To join two words with a plain **and**, use *we*: *Aýna we Merdan* (Aýna and Merdan). To contrast, use *ýöne*, **but**: *Çaý gyzgyn däl, ýöne gowy.* The tea isn't hot, but it's good.

blocks.title: Short forms
blocks.text: Only the pronouns join *hem* this way. After a name or a noun it stays a word of its own: *Aýna hem*, *kitap hem*.

summary: *däl* after a word says **not**: *Men talyp däl*. It never changes, and the pronoun stays.
`-mY` written onto a word asks a yes-no question: *-my* after a back vowel, *-mi* after a front one: *Sen ýadawmy?*, *Bu täzemi?*
The particle goes on the word you ask about: *Merdan mugallymmy?* but *Merdanmy?* After *däl*: *dälmi?*
Question words (*kim, näme, nähili, näçe, haýsy, haçan, näme üçin*) take no `-mY`.
Answer with *Hawa*, *Ýok*, *Elbetde*; *Şeýlemi?* is **really?**, and *dälmi?* after a statement is **isn't it?**
*hem* is **too**, after its word; *menem, senem, bizem, sizem*; *hem … hem* is **both … and**.
